1 Why networks?

Molecular biology is full of relations: proteins bind, kinases phosphorylate, transcription factors regulate genes, enzymes pass metabolites along, neurons synapse. A network view asks questions that a list of genes can’t answer:

  • Which proteins hold the system together (hubs and bottlenecks)?
  • Which genes work together (modules, complexes)?
  • How does a signal travel from receptor to response, and where does it loop back (pathways, feedback)?
  • How does a measurement, such as expression after a treatment, map onto that structure?

This book assumes the Kitchen for loading, querying and drawing. Its data are in the cookbooks’ data folder:

file what it is
yeast-modules.gdf 134 budding-yeast genes from seven well-known complexes and pathways (module), with the 1,320 interactions STRING scores at 0.7 or more. Edge score is STRING’s combined confidence, and experiments, databases, textmining and coexpression are the evidence behind it. From string-db.org, CC BY 4.0.
brca1-intact.gdf BRCA1’s interaction neighbourhood from IntAct: 1,228 proteins (uniprot, species, description) and 1,439 interacting pairs, with IntAct’s miscore and the number of experiments behind each (evidence). Taken from the Cytoscape export in LUMINA’s demo data. From IntAct (EMBL-EBI), CC BY 4.0.
brca2-intact.mitab The 188 IntAct records of interactions involving BRCA2 in any species, in PSI-MI TAB 2.7, as IntAct’s PSICQUIC service returns them (November 2026). From IntAct (EMBL-EBI), CC BY 4.0.
WP707-dna-damage.gpml WikiPathways’ “DNA damage response” pathway (WP707), as drawn there. From wikipathways.org, CC0.
yeast-go-slim.csv Gene Ontology slim terms for those genes (gene, aspect, term), from the Saccharomyces Genome Database, CC BY 4.0.
pheromone-pathway.csv A simplified, directed and signed map of the yeast mating-pheromone pathway, drawn from textbook accounts: who activates or inhibits whom. For teaching, not a curated resource.
pheromone-expression-SIMULATED.csv Simulated log2 fold changes at 15, 30 and 60 minutes after pheromone, for the 134 genes. They are shaped like the known response (mating genes up, G1 cyclins down) but invented: use them to learn the recipes, never as results.

2 Getting the data in

2.1 Fetch interactions for a gene list Basic

You have a list of genes (a screen’s hits, a differential-expression list). You want the known interactions among them.

Ingredients: an internet connection · makeFromSTRING

makeFromSTRING("TP53 MDM2 ATM CHEK2 CDKN1A BAX", score=0.7, add=10)
colorize(query)

How it works. makeFromSTRING(genes) asks the STRING database for interactions among the genes. species is an NCBI taxon number (9606 human, the default; 10090 mouse; 4932 yeast; 7227 fly; 6239 worm; 3702 Arabidopsis), and score is the minimum combined confidence (0.4 medium, 0.7 high, 0.9 highest). add=10 also brings in the ten proteins that interact most with your list, marked query = false. That’s how a screen’s hits get connected through genes the screen missed. Every edge records the evidence behind its score: experiments, databases, textmining, coexpression and others.

Variations. makeFromNDEx(uuid) opens a published network from the NDEx repository (Cytoscape’s network commons). Files from Cytoscape open with makeFromGraphML, makeFromGML or makeFromCSV (for SIF-like tables).

Pitfalls. A STRING edge means “associated”, not “binds”. Text mining and co-expression edges link genes that are studied together or switched on together. For physical interactions, keep the edges with strong experimental evidence, showOnly(experiments > 0.5), or build from a physical-interaction database.

2.2 Open interactions from IntAct or BioGRID Basic

You have interactions downloaded from a molecular interaction database, in the PSI-MI format they share. You want a network with the evidence behind each tie.

Ingredients: brca2-intact.mitab · makeFromFile · species · evidence

makeFromFile("brca2-intact.mitab")
colorize(species)
legendFor(species)
[(n.name, n.degree) for n in highest(degree, 3)]
len(species == "Homo sapiens")
motifLayout()

How it works. IntAct, BioGRID, MINT and the other IMEx databases export interactions as PSI-MI TAB (“MITAB”): one line per experiment, each naming two interactors, the detection method, the publication and a confidence score. makeFromFile recognises the format whatever the file is called (here makeFromMITAB would do the same). Proteins are named by gene name, with ident, taxid, species and aliases. Repeated evidence for the same pair becomes one edge, with how many records support it in evidence, the methods and publications joined with |, and IntAct’s miscore; makeFromMITAB(file, merge=false) keeps one edge per record.

The 188 records give 101 proteins and 99 interactions. Human BRCA2 (BRCA2_P51587) has 78 partners; 78 of the proteins are human, the rest come from experiments in mice, flies, plants and other organisms. Most of the ties come from co-immunoprecipitation with a tagged bait.

Pitfalls. One gene can appear as several interactors: human BRCA2 as the protein (BRCA2_P51587) and as its gene (BRCA2_ENSG00000139618), and its counterparts in other species. Names that clash get their identifier added, so check aliases before merging them with mergeNodes.

2.3 Open the yeast network and add measurements Basic

makeFromGDF("yeast-modules.gdf")
makeFromCSV("pheromone-expression-SIMULATED.csv")
FUS1.description, FUS1.lfc60

How it works. The second file is a node table (an Id column plus values), so GUESS adds its columns to the matching nodes instead of replacing the graph (Kitchen: Add attributes from a second table). The same works for any per-gene table: expression, essentiality, abundance, mutation counts. Gene names must match node names. Check the message (“134 updated”), since unmatched IDs become new, unconnected nodes.

3 Hubs and bottlenecks

3.1 Find the hubs Basic

makeFromGDF("yeast-modules.gdf")
plotDistrib(degree)
[(n.name, n.module, n.degree) for n in sortBy(degree)[-5:]]

How it works. In most molecular networks a few proteins have many partners and most have few. plotDistrib shows the shape. The biggest hubs here are proteasome subunits (RPN11 has 45 partners), because a large complex makes every member a partner of many others. The cell-cycle kinase CDC28 is the only hub outside a complex.

Pitfalls. Hubs are partly an artefact of attention: well-studied proteins have more recorded interactions. Compare against experiments evidence, or against a less biased data source, before concluding that a hub is biologically central.

3.2 Find the bottlenecks between modules Intermediate

You want the proteins that connect otherwise separate parts of the network, which are often signalling or regulatory links.

makeFromGDF("yeast-modules.gdf")
colorize(module)
legendFor(module)
sizeBy(betweenness, 6, 40)
forceAtlas2Layout()
interEdges(module).color = gray
[(n.name, n.module, round(n.betweenness)) for n in sortBy(betweenness)[-6:]]

How it works. High betweenness means many shortest paths run through a protein. Here the list mixes two kinds of bottleneck. RPN11 (proteasome) and RPS3 (ribosome) are hubs of big complexes that touch many others. CDC28, FAR1 and SKP1 sit where modules meet. FAR1 is the pheromone response’s link to the cell cycle: all 11 of its partners outside its own module are cell-cycle proteins.

Variations. mixingMatrix(module) counts the edges between each pair of modules. The largest cross-module count here is proteasome–ribosome (48), and 41 of those edges have strong experimental evidence. That isn’t necessarily function: very abundant complexes tend to turn up together in pull-down experiments. Check the evidence channels before reading a cross-module edge as cross-talk.

4 Modules and complexes

4.1 Find modules and name them Intermediate

You want groups of genes that work together, and to know what each group does.

Ingredients: yeast-modules.gdf, yeast-go-slim.csv · leidenClusters · readSets · enrichment

makeFromGDF("yeast-modules.gdf")
leidenClusters()
go = readSets("yeast-go-slim.csv", item="gene", set="term",
              where={"aspect": "process"})
r = enrichment(leiden_class == 0, go, top=5)

How it works. leidenClusters() finds communities (Kitchen: Communities). readSets reads a table with one row per gene and term into a dictionary of gene sets. where= keeps only biological-process terms. enrichment(nodes, sets) asks, for each term, whether the community has more of its genes than chance. For each term it reports:

column meaning
k/n community genes with the term / annotated community genes
K/N genes with the term / annotated genes overall
fold (k/n) ÷ (K/N): how over-represented
p the chance of so many or more by chance (hypergeometric)
q the false discovery rate over all terms tested (Benjamini–Hochberg)

The largest community has 28 of its 31 genes in “protein catabolic process” (q ≈ 2e-15): it’s the proteasome. r holds every row, and r[0]["members"] is a set of the genes, so r[0]["members"].color = red shows them.

Variations. Name every community at once:

makeFromGDF("yeast-modules.gdf")
leidenClusters()
go = readSets("yeast-go-slim.csv", item="gene", set="term",
              where={"aspect": "process"})
for grp in groupBy(leiden_class):
    best = enrichment(grp, go, show=False)[0]
    print(grp[0].leiden_class, len(grp), best["set"], "%.0e" % best["q"])

Pitfalls.

  • Choose the background deliberately. By default it’s every node that has at least one annotation. Against the whole genome, everything in a hand-picked network looks enriched. Pass background= to choose.
  • These data are unrealistically clean. The genes were picked from known complexes, so communities match them exactly (compareClusters(leiden_class, module) is 1.0). Real gene lists give messier modules, and that’s when enrichment earns its keep.

4.2 Find protein complexes with MCODE and MCL Intermediate

You want the tightly knit complexes in an interaction network, the way Cytoscape users do with MCODE or MCL.

Ingredients: yeast-modules.gdf · mcodeClusters · mclClusters · compareClusters

makeFromGDF("yeast-modules.gdf")
mcodeClusters()
colorize(mcode_class)
(mcode_class == 0).labelvisible = true
[(c, len(mcode_class == c), sorted({n.module for n in (mcode_class == c)})) for c in range(4)]

How it works. MCODE (Bader and Hogue, 2003) was designed for protein networks. It weights each protein by how dense the core of its neighbourhood is, grows complexes outward from the heaviest seeds, and scores each complex by density × size. Here it finds nine; the best (mcode_class == 0, score 31) is the proteasome, all 31 of its genes, and the next is the small ribosomal subunit. mcode_score holds each protein’s weight. Four proteins belong to no complex (mcode_class == -1).

MCL (van Dongen, 2000) takes a different route: it simulates random walks, alternately spreading them out and sharpening them, until the flow stays inside clusters. Every protein ends up in exactly one cluster:

makeFromGDF("yeast-modules.gdf")
mclClusters(inflation=2)
compareClusters(mcl_class, module)

Variations. Higher inflation gives more, smaller clusters. MCODE’s fluff=true adds the dense neighbours of each complex, and haircut=false keeps proteins with a single tie into it.

Pitfalls.

  • These modules are easy. MCL reproduces the seven modules exactly (compareClusters is 1.0), because the genes were chosen from well-known complexes. MCODE splits the cell-cycle genes into three complexes and merges one with the pheromone pathway, which is closer to what real data look like: the complexes it reports are dense cores, not whole pathways.
  • MCL needs memory. It refuses connected pieces of more than 3,000 proteins; filter by score first on big networks.

4.3 Untangle a bait-and-prey network Intermediate

You have interactions from pull-down experiments: a few bait proteins, each with dozens of partners found only with it. You want a drawing in which every protein can be seen.

Ingredients: brca1-intact.gdf · motifLayout · motif · encircleBy

makeFromGDF("brca1-intact.gdf")
motifLayout(outline=true)
[(n.name, n.degree) for n in highest(degree, 4)]
len([n for n in g.nodes if n.motif.startswith("star")])

How it works. A force layout pulls every partner of a bait towards it, so a bait with 100 partners becomes a solid blob. motifLayout() (a port of LUMINA, the IntAct team’s layout) recognises the shapes that cause this: a protein with partners that have no other partners is a star, drawn with those partners in rings around it; proteins that share exactly the same partners are parallel and line up in a grid between them; cycles become circles and chains small rings. Each shape is laid out as one large node, so the drawing still keeps the distances of the network, and the 17 separate pieces are packed side by side. Here 46 stars hold 1,052 of the 1,228 proteins: BRCA1 itself (BRCA1_P38398) has 275 partners, then PHF11, BAP1 and NBR1. The field motif says which shape each protein is in.

Variations. colorize(motif) colours the shapes instead of outlining them; motifLayout(spacing=40) spreads each shape out; minStar=5 keeps hubs with fewer leaves out of the star treatment.

Pitfalls.

  • It’s for sparse, hub-rich networks. On dense ones such as yeast-modules.gdf, built from complexes where everyone binds everyone, it finds almost no shapes and draws like a plain stress layout.
  • Merge repeated evidence first. IntAct and STRING exports often list one pair many times; simplify() merges them, or the repeats are drawn as bundles of curves.

5 Pathways and regulation

5.1 Open a pathway from WikiPathways or KEGG Basic

You want a curated pathway diagram as a network you can analyse, drawn as its curators drew it.

Ingredients: WP707-dna-damage.gpml · makeFromFile · kind · arrow

makeFromFile("WP707-dna-damage.gpml")
center()
(arrow == "TBar").color = red
[n.label for n in g.nodes if n.kind == "GeneProduct"][:8]

How it works. WikiPathways stores its pathways as GPML, PathVisio’s format; makeFromFile (or makeFromGPML) keeps the positions, sizes and colours of the diagram. Each box becomes a node with its kind (GeneProduct, Metabolite, Pathway, …) and database cross-reference, and each line a directed edge whose arrow says what it means: here 75 arrows (activation, conversion) and 22 “T bars” (inhibition), coloured red above. Where a line ends on another line, as a catalysis does on a reaction, GUESS puts a small anchor node; lines that end on nothing get a small point node, so no edge is lost.

Variations. KEGG maps (KGML, from the KEGG API) open the same way, as do SBML models (BioModels) and BioPAX pathways (Reactome, Pathway Commons):

makeFromFile("hsa04115.xml")                 # KEGG p53 signalling (KGML)
makeFromFile("BIOMD0000000010.xml")          # an SBML model: species and reactions
makeFromBioPAX("R-HSA-69620.owl")            # a Reactome pathway, as a simple network

Pitfalls. A pathway diagram is a drawing: some boxes stand for groups or other pathways (kind “group” or “Pathway”), and a gene can appear twice. removeNode the decorations, or mergeNodes the repeats, before measuring centrality.

5.2 Draw a signalling pathway Basic

You have a directed, signed pathway. You want a readable picture, from receptor to response.

Ingredients: pheromone-pathway.csv · dotLayout · edge queries

makeFromCSV("pheromone-pathway.csv")
labelBy(name)
g.nodes.labelpos = "inside"
fitNodesToLabels()
dotLayout()
(effect == "inhibits").color = red
(effect == "activates").color = darkgray
STE2.color = orange
STE12.color = purple

How it works. dotLayout() (Graphviz) ranks nodes top to bottom by following the arrows. Feedback edges point back up, which makes loops easy to spot. fitNodesToLabels() sizes each node to hold its name. Do it before the layout, so the layout leaves room for the bigger nodes.

Variations. descendants(STE2) is everything downstream of the receptor. ancestors(CDC28) is everything that can influence the cell-cycle kinase. shortestPath(STE2, CDC28) is the most direct route.

5.3 Find the feedback loops Advanced

You want the cycles in a pathway, and whether each one amplifies the signal (positive feedback) or damps it (negative feedback).

makeFromCSV("pheromone-pathway.csv")
import networkx as nx
G = toNetworkX()
for cyc in sorted(nx.simple_cycles(G), key=len)[:6]:
    steps = list(zip(cyc, cyc[1:] + cyc[:1]))
    signs = [G.edges[a, b]["effect"] for a, b in steps]
    kind = "negative" if signs.count("inhibits") % 2 else "positive"
    print(kind, " -> ".join(cyc))

How it works. toNetworkX() hands the graph to networkx, whose simple_cycles lists every cycle. A loop’s sign is the product of its edges’ signs, so an odd number of inhibitions makes it negative. The shortest loop, FUS3 → STE12 → MSG5 -| FUS3, is negative: the response switches on a phosphatase that turns the kinase off. The loop through the receptor (STE12 → STE2) is positive: responding cells make more receptor.

Pitfalls. Real pathways have many overlapping cycles (24 in this small map). List the shortest, and look at which edges they share: feedbackEdges() gives the fewest edges whose removal breaks every cycle.

6 Measurements on the network

6.1 Colour genes by expression Basic

makeFromGDF("yeast-modules.gdf")
makeFromCSV("pheromone-expression-SIMULATED.csv")
forceAtlas2Layout()
colorBy(lfc60, blue, red, center=0)
legendFor(lfc60)

How it works. colorBy(field, low, high) maps numbers to a gradient. center=0 makes it diverging: zero is white, and the two ends are equally far from zero, so a gene down 2 is as deep a blue as a gene up 2 is red. That’s the right choice for fold changes, where zero means “no change” and both directions matter.

Pitfalls. Without center=, a three-colour gradient puts its middle colour halfway between the lowest and highest values. Here the values run from −3.0 to 4.4, so “white” would fall at +0.7 and every unchanged gene would be tinted. Always pin the centre for signed data.

6.2 Animate a time course Intermediate

makeFromGDF("yeast-modules.gdf")
makeFromCSV("pheromone-expression-SIMULATED.csv")
forceAtlas2Layout()
for t in (lfc15, lfc30, lfc60):
    colorBy(t, blue, red, center=0)
    ss(t.name)
ls("lfc15")
morph("lfc30", 1500)

How it works. Each time point is saved as a state with its own colours, and morph animates between them, so the response is seen spreading through the network. addSlide instead of ss makes a presentation. To show all time points at once, pieChart([lfc15, lfc30, lfc60]) draws each gene as a pie of its values. Pies work best with positive amounts (abundances, counts), not signed changes.

7 Case studies

7.1 A protein’s contact network Intermediate

You want to see a protein’s fold as a network, and find the residues that hold it together.

makeFromPDB("1ubq.pdb")
colorize(structure)
legendFor(structure)
sizeBy(betweenness, 6, 26)
(kind == "chain").color = "120,120,120"
sortBy(betweenness, descending=True)[:6]

How it works. makeFromPDB reads a structure file (or downloads a four-character PDB id from RCSB) and makes one node per amino acid. Two residues are joined if they follow each other along the chain (kind “chain”) or if their alpha carbons are closer than cutoff angstroms (default 8; kind “contact”, with the distance). Nodes carry residue, the one-letter aa, the position seq, the structure (helix, strand or coil, from the file’s HELIX and SHEET records) and the 3D position. They are placed by the structure’s two main directions, so the picture looks like the folded protein.

Ubiquitin (1ubq) has 76 residues, 75 chain links and 251 contacts. The residues with the highest betweenness, the ones most shortest paths run through, are in the hydrophobic core between the helix and the sheet: LEU15, LEU50, GLN41, LEU69, ILE23 and ILE30. Residue networks like this are used to find residues that pass signals across a protein (allostery) and those whose mutation would most disturb the fold.

Pitfalls. The picture is a 2D shadow of a 3D object: residues that look close may not be, so trust the edges, not the distances on screen. The contact network depends on cutoff; 7 to 8.5 Å is usual.

7.2 The worm’s wiring Intermediate

You want a first look at a whole nervous system: who sends signals, who receives them, and the hubs.

makeFromFile("celegans-neural.gdf")
g.edges.width = 0.4                       # thin connections, so the neurons show
g.edges.color = "150,150,150,60"
sizeBy(degree, 3, 24)
colorBy(outdegree, "200,210,240", "200,40,40")
plotFrequency(degree, cumulative=True, log=True)
plotSpectrum("adjacency")

How it works. This is the neural network of the worm C. elegans (White et al. 1986, as compiled by Watts and Strogatz): 297 neurons and 2,345 directed connections, with weight the number of synapses (1 to 70). The mean neuron has 15.8 connections, but a few have far more: n305 receives 134 and sends none (signals end there), and n71 and n72 have 83 and 80, about half in, half out. plotFrequency(degree, cumulative=True, log=True) shows the heavy tail.

plotSpectrum("adjacency") charts the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix (direction ignored). The largest, 24.4, stands well clear of the next (14.2): one dominant pattern of connection, centred on the hubs. It is close to, but below, ⟨k²⟩/⟨k⟩ = 28, the value it would have if neurons were wired at random with these degrees. spectrum() gives the numbers; the Laplacian’s (the default) has a single zero, so the network is in one piece.

Pitfalls. The neurons are named by number (n1 to n306, as in Watts and Strogatz’s version), not by their biological names. Weights count synapses, so a single connection can stand for many; sizeBy(weight) on the edges shows them.

7.3 Case study: how pheromone stops the cell cycle Intermediate

A haploid yeast cell that senses mating pheromone stops dividing in G1, so it can fuse with a partner. Starting from the network alone, how does the signal reach the cell-cycle machinery?

makeFromGDF("yeast-modules.gdf")
colorize(module)
p = shortestPath(STE2, CDC28)
[n.name for n in p if n in g.nodes]

In the STRING network the shortest route from the receptor STE2 to the cyclin-dependent kinase CDC28 runs through BEM1, a polarity scaffold shared by mating and budding. Shortest paths in an association network are suggestive, not mechanistic: an association can be any kind of link.

showOnly((module == "pheromone response") | (module == "cell cycle"))
forceAtlas2Layout()
sizeBy(betweenness, 6, 40)
bridging = interEdges(module)
bridging.color = red
ends = [n for e in bridging for n in (e.node1, e.node2)]
sorted(set(n.name for n in ends if n.module == "pheromone response"))

The 28 edges between the two modules touch ten pheromone genes, but FAR1 alone accounts for 11 of them, all to cell-cycle proteins. That points to the known mechanism (FUS3 activates FAR1, which inhibits CDC28 with its G1 cyclins), which the directed pathway map makes explicit:

makeFromCSV("pheromone-pathway.csv")
[n.name for n in shortestPath(STE2, CDC28) if n in g.nodes]

Following the arrows, the route is STE2 → STE4 → STE5 → FUS3 → FAR1 -| CDC28: receptor, G-protein, scaffold, MAP kinase, then the CDK inhibitor.

7.4 Case study: from a hit list to modules Advanced

A screen gives you genes. With a network connection, the full workflow is:

hits = "RPN11 RPT5 PRE1 CDC28 CLN2 FAR1 FUS3 STE12 RPO21 MSH2"
makeFromSTRING(hits, species=4932, add=20)
leidenClusters()

The bundled network stands in for that result here:

makeFromGDF("yeast-modules.gdf")
subgraph(experiments > 0.5, "physical")
leidenClusters()
go = readSets("yeast-go-slim.csv", item="gene", set="term",
              where={"aspect": "process"})
for grp in groupBy(leiden_class)[:5]:
    best = enrichment(grp, go, show=False)[0]
    print(len(grp), best["set"], "q=%.0e" % best["q"])

subgraph(experiments > 0.5, "physical") opens a graph of just the edges with strong experimental evidence (1,028 of 1,320) and the genes they join (use("main") goes back). Communities are then re-found and named by their top term. Which modules survive with physical evidence alone, and which were held together by co-expression and text mining? Ask that of any network built from mixed evidence. Here all seven survive, each still enriched for the right process. With a real hit list, expect some modules to dissolve.

Pitfall. A subgraph of edges loses any gene left with no strong edge. subgraph(experiments > 0.5) keeps 134 genes here, but on noisier data count the nodes before and after, and treat those that drop out as “no physical evidence”, not “no interaction”.

8 Capstone

8.1 Capstone: a module browser for a time course Advanced

The problem. A lab has a time course after a treatment and wants to browse it through the interaction network. Which modules respond? When? Which genes lead? This recipe builds a module browser:

  • modules are found and named by their top GO term, and a drop-down picks one;
  • a slider steps through the time points, recolouring every gene;
  • a checkbox switches between all evidence and experimental evidence only;
  • a click on a gene shows its description and its values at every time point;
  • a legend shows the diverging scale.
makeFromGDF("yeast-modules.gdf")
makeFromCSV("pheromone-expression-SIMULATED.csv")
forceAtlas2Layout()
_ = leidenClusters()
go = readSets("yeast-go-slim.csv", item="gene", set="term", where={"aspect": "process"})
names = {}
for grp in groupBy(leiden_class):
    names[enrichment(grp, go, show=False)[0]["set"]] = grp[0].leiden_class
times = [lfc15, lfc30, lfc60]
state = {"t": 2}

def recolour(i):
    state["t"] = int(i)
    colorBy(times[state["t"]], blue, red, center=0)
    legendFor(times[state["t"]], title=f"log2 change at {[15, 30, 60][state['t']]} min")

def pick_module(term):
    members = (leiden_class == names[term])
    g.nodes.labelvisible = false
    members.labelvisible = true
    center(members)
    up = len(members & (times[state["t"]] > 1))
    info.text = f"{term}: {len(members)} genes, {up} up more than 2-fold"

def evidence(only):
    if only:
        showOnly(experiments > 0.5)
    else:
        showAll()

def gene(n):
    values = ", ".join(f"{t}: {getattr(n, f.name):+.1f}" for t, f in zip((15, 30, 60), times))
    info.text = f"{n.name} ({n.module}): {n.description}; {values}"

info = Label("pick a module, or click a gene")
ui.dock(Panel("Modules", Dropdown(sorted(names), label="module", onChange=pick_module),
              Slider(0, 2, 2, label="time point (15, 30, 60 min)", onChange=recolour),
              Checkbox("experimental evidence only", onChange=evidence), info, position="bottom"))
graphevents.clickNode = gene
recolour(2)
center()

How it works.

  • Naming the modules. The modules come from leidenClusters(), and each is named by its top enriched term (the module-naming recipe), so the drop-down lists biology (“signal transduction”, “protein catabolic process”), not numbers.
  • The slider. It indexes the three expression fields. colorBy(..., center=0) and legendFor redraw the diverging scale for each time point.
  • The checkbox. It toggles showOnly(experiments > 0.5), the physical-evidence view from the second case study.
  • The click. It reads a gene’s fields into the label.

As before, the expression values are simulated: substitute your own table, with an Id column of gene names, in the second line.

As an app. A capstone like this can be packaged so it opens on its own, without the console, through ?app= (manual, Apps). Help → Example apps → Interactome Explorer is one for this book: BRCA1’s interactions from IntAct, laid out by motifLayout, with tabs for exploring, colouring and filtering, the data table below and a confidence slider. Its source is web/public/apps/interactome/.
